subject: maths
title: Combined events and sample space diagrams

slides.heading: Combined events — what happens when two things occur together
slides.body: Sometimes you need the probability of two events both happening, or one or the other happening. The rule you use depends on the relationship between the events: if two events cannot happen at the same time they are mutually exclusive (e.g. rolling a 3 and rolling a 5 on one die), and you add their probabilities. If two events don't affect each other they are independent (e.g. flipping a coin and rolling a die), and you multiply their probabilities. Confusing these two rules is the single most common error in probability.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The AND rule and the OR rule
slides.formula: Independent events — AND rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)  |  Mutually exclusive events — OR rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
slides.formulaExplained: AND rule (multiply): use this when you want both events to happen and the events are independent — one outcome does not change the probability of the other. Example: P(heads) × P(rolling a 4) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. OR rule (add): use this when you want either event to happen and the events are mutually exclusive — they cannot both happen at the same time. Example: P(rolling a 2 or a 5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. Warning: the OR rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) is the general version; the simpler addition only works when A and B cannot both happen.
slides.whenToUse: Any question asking for the probability of two events both occurring (multiply if independent) or either occurring (add if mutually exclusive). A sample space diagram lists every possible combined outcome and is useful for finding probabilities by counting.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Two fair spinners each have sections numbered 1, 2 and 3. Both are spun once. Using a sample space diagram, find the probability that the two numbers add to 4.

steps.instruction: Draw the sample space: list all 3 × 3 = 9 equally likely outcomes as pairs (Spinner 1, Spinner 2).

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Adding probabilities for independent events instead of multiplying — writing P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B).
mistakes.correction: AND means multiply (for independent events). OR means add (for mutually exclusive events). 'Both happen' = multiply. 'Either happens' = add. The words tell you which rule to use.

mistakes.mistake: Using the OR rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when the events are not mutually exclusive — double-counting outcomes that are in both events.
mistakes.correction: If A and B can both happen at the same time, use the general rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Only drop the subtraction when you are certain the events are mutually exclusive.

mistakes.mistake: Missing outcomes in a sample space diagram — listing only some combinations and miscounting the total.
mistakes.correction: For two events with m and n outcomes, the sample space always has m × n entries. Draw a grid: one event along the top, one down the side. Fill every cell — don't try to list them in a column.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Independent events — AND rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Use when both events must happen and one doesn't affect the other.
keyFacts.examTip: If the question says 'both', 'and', or involves two separate trials (two coins, two dice), multiply the probabilities.

keyFacts.fact: Mutually exclusive events — OR rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Use when the events cannot both happen at the same time.
keyFacts.examTip: If the question says 'or' and the events are mutually exclusive (e.g. different faces of one die), add. Check they can't both happen before adding.

keyFacts.fact: A sample space diagram lists every possible combined outcome. The total number of outcomes = m × n (m outcomes for one event, n for the other).
keyFacts.examTip: Draw a full grid — don't list outcomes in a column where it's easy to miss some. Count every cell as a check.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
